screens.title: Firebase Authentication: Email/Password and Google Sign-In
screens.subtitle: Secure sign-in flows, reactive auth state, and Google single-tap sign-in for Flutter

narration.text: Authentication controls who uses your app and how it saves user data. In this chapter you'll see two common approaches: email and password authentication, and Google Sign-In as a social provider. We'll cover enabling providers in the Firebase Console, using the firebase_auth plugin to register and sign in users, and reacting to changes with Firebase's authStateChanges stream so your UI updates automatically. You'll also learn how to wire up google_sign_in to obtain provider credentials, and why calling signOut on both FirebaseAuth and the GoogleSignIn instance matters. Practical error handling is emphasized: catching FirebaseAuthException codes like weak-password, email-already-in-use, user-not-found, and wrong-password lets you give clear feedback instead of failing silently. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to implement registration and login flows, add Google as an alternative, and keep the UI in sync with the user's session. As you watch code run, pay attention to awaiting asynchronous calls and to enabling sign-in providers in the Firebase Console — missing that toggle is a common source of frustrating errors. What first screen will your user see when authStateChanges emits null or a User? We'll show that pattern and the concrete code next.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use firebase_auth to register and sign in users, listen to authStateChanges for reactive UI, and integrate google_sign_in to accept Google accounts safely.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Overview
Firebase Authentication
Implement Email/Password and Google Sign-In with firebase_auth and google_sign_in.

This lesson shows how to register and authenticate users, update your UI when the user signs in or out, and integrate Google Sign-In to provide a faster login path. We keep security and UX in mind by catching FirebaseAuthException codes and awaiting sign-in results before reading currentUser.

You will see concrete code snippets for creating accounts, signing in, listening to auth state changes with StreamBuilder, and pairing Google credentials with Firebase.

What you'll be able to do

Register/login with email, add Google Sign-In, handle errors, and keep your UI reactive to auth state.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll practice and why it matters

narration.text: In this lesson we focus on four measurable objectives that map to building secure, reactive authentication in Flutter. First, you will implement user registration and login using Firebase Email/Password Authentication so users can create and access accounts. Second, you will handle authentication state changes using Firebase's authStateChanges stream so the UI reflects whether a user is signed in. Third, you will integrate Google Sign-In as an alternate provider, learning how to obtain provider tokens and convert them to Firebase credentials. Fourth, you will manage sessions and sign users out safely, including clearing any Google session to avoid accidental reauth. Each objective pairs code with validation and error handling so your app remains robust and user-friendly. These skills matter because most apps require identity, and correct async handling and provider configuration prevent subtle bugs and poor UX. As you work, think about the notifications, error messages, and state transitions your users will see.

keyIdea.title: Measured practice
keyIdea.text: Implement register/login, react to auth state, add Google sign-in, and manage sign-out with clear error handling.

screens.title: Skills and Error Handling Objectives
screens.subtitle: Practical skills to make authentication robust and user-friendly

narration.text: Beyond basic mechanics, you will learn to handle asynchronous behavior and common error scenarios. Properly awaiting sign-in and registration calls prevents race conditions where currentUser is read before Firebase finishes initializing. You'll practice wrapping createUserWithEmailAndPassword and signInWithEmailAndPassword in try-catch blocks that inspect FirebaseAuthException codes like weak-password, email-already-in-use, invalid-email, user-not-found, and wrong-password. Another objective is to manage the Google session: calling signOut on the GoogleSignIn instance ensures users are prompted to choose an account on the next sign-in attempt. Lastly, you'll practice initializing Firebase in main so services are available. These skills reduce user confusion and avoid crashes in production. As you study examples, compare what happens when a provider isn't enabled in the Console versus when the code is incorrect — the Console toggle is a common oversight and causes operation-not-allowed type errors.

keyIdea.title: Error-first mindset
keyIdea.text: Expect provider configuration and async edge cases; use try-catch for FirebaseAuthException and clear sign-out steps for provider sessions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Handling Errors
Handle FirebaseAuthException
Wrap auth calls in try-catch and inspect e.code to provide helpful messages.
weak-password → prompt stronger password
email-already-in-use → offer sign-in instead of re-register
invalid-email/user-not-found/wrong-password → clear user-facing message
Async and Provider Mistakes
Common pitfalls include reading currentUser before awaiting sign-in and forgetting to enable a provider in the Firebase Console.
Quick checks
  • Confirm Email/Password and Google are enabled in Console.
  • Await authentication calls before accessing currentUser.
  • Call googleSignIn.signOut() when signing out users who used Google.
Example
If createUserWithEmailAndPassword returns a weak-password error, show a validation hint and keep the user on the registration form instead of navigating away.
Key takeaway
Anticipate provider configuration issues and treat FirebaseAuthException codes as the main source for user-facing error text.

screens.title: Why Firebase Authentication?
screens.subtitle: Definition and practical role in your app

narration.text: Firebase Authentication is a backend service that manages user identities and provides secure authentication methods such as email/password and social logins. As a definition, it abstracts password hashing, session management, and account recovery so you can avoid rolling your own authentication logic. Practically, that means less surface area for security bugs and a faster path to delivering features that rely on user identity, like personalized content or saved preferences. For example, instead of implementing password storage and reset flows yourself, you call createUserWithEmailAndPassword and rely on Firebase's account lifecycle, which returns a UserCredential you can use immediately. A common misconception is that Firebase handles all app authorization; it provides authentication and user identity, but you still design rules and checks for what authenticated users are allowed to do. Another misconception is that using firebase_auth removes the need to initialize Firebase; you must still call Firebase. initializeApp during startup or none of the services will work. Takeaway: Firebase Authentication offers a secure, managed identity layer, but you must wire it into your app lifecycle and authorization model deliberately. How will you use the User object to personalize your app once sign-in succeeds?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Firebase Authentication provides managed identity services so your app can register, sign in, and maintain user sessions without custom password storage.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Why Firebase Auth?
What it does
Handles sign-up, sign-in, token management, and integrations with identity providers so you can focus on app logic.
• Managed password hashing and account recovery reduce security burden.
• UserCredential holds the authenticated user and metadata you can use immediately.
• You still design access rules and check user identity in your app and backend.
Key takeaway
Use Firebase Authentication to offload identity management but keep explicit initialization and authorization checks in your code.
Concrete example
Register a user with createUserWithEmailAndPassword, read the returned UserCredential, and store the uid in Firestore for personalized data.
// Example: registration call flow (conceptual)
final FirebaseAuth _auth = FirebaseAuth.instance;
UserCredential userCredential = await _auth.createUserWithEmailAndPassword(
  email: 'you@example.com',
  password: 'SuperSecret123',
);
print('User registered: ' + (userCredential.user?.email ?? 'unknown'));
Misconception: FirebaseAuth does not grant authorization rules automatically. Define what an authenticated user can access, for example by using Firestore security rules keyed by uid.

screens.title: Enable Authentication Providers in Firebase Console
screens.subtitle: Configure Email/Password and Google before you run the app

narration.text: Before your code can authenticate users, the providers you intend to use must be enabled in the Firebase Console. This is a configuration step many learners miss, and it produces an 'Operation not allowed' or other confusing errors if skipped. For Email/Password you simply toggle the provider on under Authentication → Sign-in method. For Google Sign-In you must set a support email and, for production, configure OAuth consent and client IDs for Android and iOS. If you used flutterfire configure earlier, the generated firebase_options. dart will often include the correct client IDs, but you should confirm the Console settings match your project. Concrete example: enabling Email/Password allows createUserWithEmailAndPassword to succeed; leaving it off makes the same call fail even though your code is correct. A common misconception is that package installation alone is enough; provider toggles in the Console are a separate requirement. Always double-check provider toggles and any required OAuth client information when adding third-party sign-in methods. Takeaway: configuration in the Console is as important as code — treat them as paired steps. Enable Authentication Providers in Firebase Console means provider toggles in firebase console are mandatory. without enabling email/password or google you will get operation-not-allowed or similar errors even when code is correct.. In practical terms, configure email/password and google before you run the app. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Enable providers first
keyIdea.text: Provider toggles in Firebase Console are mandatory. Without enabling Email/Password or Google you will get operation-not-allowed or similar errors even when code is correct.

screens.title: Register and Sign In with Email/Password
screens.subtitle: Create accounts and handle FirebaseAuthException errors

narration.text: Let's walk through the core code for Email/Password registration and login using the firebase_auth package. The pattern is consistent: call the asynchronous A P I, await the result, and wrap it in a try-catch that checks FirebaseAuthException codes. As an example, createUserWithEmailAndPassword returns a UserCredential on success; if the password is too weak you receive a weak-password code, and if the email already exists you get email-already-in-use. For sign-in, signInWithEmailAndPassword will throw user-not-found or wrong-password when credentials don't match. A common mistake is not awaiting these calls, then reading FirebaseAuth. instance. currentUser immediately; that can return null and cause UI glitches. Always show clear messages for each code so users know whether to correct input or recover an account. Concrete example: in registerWithEmailPassword, print or display the created user email from userCredential. user?. email, and if a weak-password code is caught, prompt for a stronger password. Takeaway: these methods are simple but rely on correct async handling and explicit error mapping to good UX. Register and Sign In with Email/Password means await createuserwithemailandpassword or signinwithemailandpassword and handle firebaseauthexception codes to provide clear feedback.. In practical terms, create accounts and handle firebaseauthexception errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Await createUserWithEmailAndPassword or signInWithEmailAndPassword and handle FirebaseAuthException codes to provide clear feedback.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Email/Password Code
Registration example
// Example for Email/Password Registration
import 'package:firebase_auth/firebase_auth.dart';

final FirebaseAuth _auth = FirebaseAuth.instance;

Future registerWithEmailPassword(String email, String password) async {
  try {
    UserCredential userCredential = await _auth.createUserWithEmailAndPassword(
      email: email,
      password: password,
    );
    print('User registered: ${userCredential.user?.email}');
  } on FirebaseAuthException catch (e) {
    if (e.code == 'weak-password') {
      print('The password provided is too weak.');
    } else if (e.code == 'email-already-in-use') {
      print('The account already exists for that email.');
    } else {
      print('Registration error: ${e.message}');
    }
  } catch (e) {
    print(e);
  }
}
Sign-in example
// Example for Email/Password Login
Future signInWithEmailPassword(String email, String password) async {
  try {
    UserCredential userCredential = await _auth.signInWithEmailAndPassword(
      email: email,
      password: password,
    );
    print('User signed in: ${userCredential.user?.email}');
  } on FirebaseAuthException catch (e) {
    if (e.code == 'user-not-found') {
      print('No user found for that email.');
    } else if (e.code == 'wrong-password') {
      print('Wrong password provided for that user.');
    } else {
      print('Login error: ${e.message}');
    }
  } catch (e) {
    print(e);
  }
}
Pro tip
Display friendly messages for each FirebaseAuthException code instead of raw exception text to help users recover.

screens.title: Auth State and Reactive UI
screens.subtitle: Use authStateChanges and StreamBuilder to switch screens

narration.text: A common architecture pattern for authentication in Flutter is to use FirebaseAuth. instance. authStateChanges with a StreamBuilder as the app root to choose which screen to display. The stream emits a User object when signed in or null when signed out. Using StreamBuilder ensures your UI responds immediately to sign-in, sign-out, or profile changes without manual navigation code. For example, build the AuthWrapper widget that returns a CircularProgressIndicator while waiting, HomeScreen when snapshot. hasData, and AuthScreen otherwise. A common misconception is to use FutureBuilder with currentUser; that only reflects the user at a single moment and will not update when the user signs out elsewhere. Another pitfall is not awaiting Firebase. initializeApp before subscribing to authStateChanges — this leads to errors or an initial null user. Concrete example: when the stream emits null the wrapper shows the AuthScreen where createUserWithEmailAndPassword is available; when it emits a User, the wrapper shows HomeScreen, which can display FirebaseAuth. instance. currentUser?. email. Takeaway: StreamBuilder + authStateChanges is the recommended reactive pattern to keep your app in sync with authentication state. Auth State and Reactive UI means use authstatechanges with streambuilder so the ui updates automatically when the authentication state changes.. In practical terms, use authstatechanges and streambuilder to switch screens. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reactive pattern
keyIdea.text: Use authStateChanges with StreamBuilder so the UI updates automatically when the authentication state changes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Auth State
AuthWrapper pattern
return StreamBuilder(
  stream: FirebaseAuth.instance.authStateChanges(),
  builder: (context, snapshot) {
    if (snapshot.connectionState == ConnectionState.waiting) {
      return const CircularProgressIndicator();
    }
    if (snapshot.hasData) {
      return const HomeScreen();
    }
    return const AuthScreen();
  },
);
This structure avoids manual navigation when users sign in or out, and centralizes the decision of which top-level screen to show.
Common mistakes & fixes
  • Don't use FutureBuilder with currentUser; it won't update on sign-out.
  • Initialize Firebase before listening to authStateChanges to avoid race conditions.
  • Show a loading state while the stream connection is waiting to avoid flicker.
Key takeaway
StreamBuilder with authStateChanges is the dependable way to present the correct top-level screen for the user's session state.

screens.title: Integrate Google Sign-In
screens.subtitle: Obtain tokens with google_sign_in and sign into Firebase

narration.text: Google Sign-In provides a quicker login for users who already have Google accounts on their device. The flow uses the google_sign_in package to present an account chooser and return authentication tokens. You then convert those tokens into a Firebase credential with GoogleAuthProvider. credential and pass it to signInWithCredential. Concretely: call GoogleSignIn(). signIn(), obtain googleUser?. authentication, check for null in case the user cancelled, then create the credential and await _auth. signInWithCredential(credential). Handle FirebaseAuthException and general errors similarly to email/password flows. A frequent oversight is not adding google_sign_in to pubspec. yaml or not configuring OAuth client IDs in the Console for Android and iOS; both are required for a smooth flow. Also consider calling _googleSignIn. signOut() on sign-out to clear the local Google session. Misconception: google_sign_in replaces firebase_auth — it complements it. Firebase still authenticates and issues the User object. Takeaway: exchange provider tokens for Firebase credentials and treat cancellation and token absence as normal control paths you handle gracefully. Integrate Google Sign-In means use google_sign_in to get tokens, then sign in to firebase with signinwithcredential using googleauthprovider credentials.. In practical terms, obtain tokens with google_sign_in and sign into firebase. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Google flow
keyIdea.text: Use google_sign_in to get tokens, then sign in to Firebase with signInWithCredential using GoogleAuthProvider credentials.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Google Sign-In
Google sign-in example
// Example for Google Sign-In
import 'package:google_sign_in/google_sign_in.dart';
import 'package:firebase_auth/firebase_auth.dart';

final GoogleSignIn _googleSignIn = GoogleSignIn();
final FirebaseAuth _auth = FirebaseAuth.instance;

Future signInWithGoogle() async {
  try {
    final GoogleSignInAccount? googleUser = await _googleSignIn.signIn();

    final GoogleSignInAuthentication? googleAuth = await googleUser?.authentication;

    if (googleAuth == null) {
      return null; // User cancelled
    }

    final credential = GoogleAuthProvider.credential(
      accessToken: googleAuth.accessToken,
      idToken: googleAuth.idToken,
    );

    final UserCredential userCredential = await _auth.signInWithCredential(credential);
    print('Signed in with Google: ${userCredential.user?.displayName}');
    return userCredential.user;
  } on FirebaseAuthException catch (e) {
    print('Firebase Auth Error during Google Sign-In: ${e.message}');
    return null;
  } catch (e) {
    print('Error during Google Sign-In: $e');
    return null;
  }
}
Notes and best practices
  • Add google_sign_in to pubspec.yaml and run flutter pub get.
  • Verify OAuth client IDs in the Firebase Console for each platform.
  • Handle the null authentication case when the user cancels the account chooser.
  • Clear the Google session on sign-out to force account choice next time.
Key takeaway
Google Sign-In improves UX but requires both package setup and Console configuration; treat it as a complement to firebase_auth, not a replacement.

screens.title: Signing Out and Session Management
screens.subtitle: End sessions safely and clear provider state

narration.text: Signing users out must do two things: invalidate the Firebase session and, when relevant, clear any provider-specific session so the next sign-in prompts account selection. The Firebase call is simple: await FirebaseAuth. instance. signOut(). This triggers authStateChanges to emit null so StreamBuilder can show the login screen. For Google Sign-In, call _googleSignIn. signOut() in addition to FirebaseAuth signOut; otherwise, the Google account may remain cached and a subsequent sign-in might skip the chooser. A concrete example: when the user taps sign out on HomeScreen, call await FirebaseAuth. instance. signOut(); then await _googleSignIn. signOut(); if the user used Google. A typical misconception is that a single FirebaseAuth. signOut clears provider sessions; it does not clear the local GoogleSignIn state. Another practical note: signOut is asynchronous — await it before navigating or updating UI to avoid race conditions. Takeaway: make sign-out explicit for each provider you support and use authStateChanges to update the UI reliably after sign-out completes. Signing Out and Session Management means call firebaseauth.signout and provider-specific signout (e.g., googlesignin.signout) to fully clear sessions and trigger authstatechanges.. In practical terms, end sessions safely and clear provider state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Sign-out pattern
keyIdea.text: Call FirebaseAuth.signOut and provider-specific signOut (e.g., GoogleSignIn.signOut) to fully clear sessions and trigger authStateChanges.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Sign Out
Sign-out steps
Always await signOut calls and clear provider sessions when present.
1. await FirebaseAuth.instance.signOut()
2. If using Google, await _googleSignIn.signOut()
3. Rely on authStateChanges to switch to AuthScreen
Example (HomeScreen)
Call signOut from a tap handler and await it. Only after signOut completes should you assume currentUser is null or the StreamBuilder will reflect the change.
Common mistake
Not clearing provider session leaves automatic re-login behavior that confuses users who expect to choose accounts again.

screens.title: Build AuthScreen and AuthWrapper
screens.subtitle: Wire forms, controllers, and StreamBuilder together

narration.text: This hands-on activity ties the concepts into a runnable implementation. Create an AuthScreen with TextEditingController instances for email and password, and buttons to register and sign in that call your try-catch wrappers. Implement _register and _signIn to call the firebase_auth methods and set an _errorMessage state when exceptions occur so the user sees clear feedback. Then update main to initialize Firebase and set the home to AuthWrapper, which listens to authStateChanges and returns HomeScreen or AuthScreen accordingly. A concrete example is provided in the chapter: AuthScreen manages controllers and calls FirebaseAuth. instance. createUserWithEmailAndPassword in _register. A common error is forgetting to dispose controllers or to mark async functions with await in the button handlers; this can cause memory leaks or incorrect UI timing. After implementing, run the app, register a new email and password, confirm HomeScreen shows the user email, then sign out and verify the wrapper returns to AuthScreen. Takeaway: the activity demonstrates how UI, controllers, and the authentication stream all work together in a complete flow. Build AuthScreen and AuthWrapper means build authscreen with controllers and authwrapper using authstatechanges to create a complete register/login flow and test sign-out transitions.. In practical terms, wire forms, controllers, and streambuilder together. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical assembly
keyIdea.text: Build AuthScreen with controllers and AuthWrapper using authStateChanges to create a complete register/login flow and test sign-out transitions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › AuthScreen / AuthWrapper
AuthScreen (concept)
// AuthScreen: controllers and handlers
final TextEditingController _emailController = TextEditingController();
final TextEditingController _passwordController = TextEditingController();

Future _register() async {
  try {
    await FirebaseAuth.instance.createUserWithEmailAndPassword(
      email: _emailController.text,
      password: _passwordController.text,
    );
  } on FirebaseAuthException catch (e) {
    setState(() => _errorMessage = e.message);
  }
}
Main / AuthWrapper
// main.dart initialization and wrapper
void main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  await Firebase.initializeApp(options: DefaultFirebaseOptions.currentPlatform);
  runApp(const MyApp());
}

class AuthWrapper extends StatelessWidget {
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return StreamBuilder(
      stream: FirebaseAuth.instance.authStateChanges(),
      builder: (context, snapshot) { /* show HomeScreen or AuthScreen */ },
    );
  }
}
Testing checklist: register a new user, confirm HomeScreen shows email, sign out, and ensure wrapper returns to AuthScreen.

screens.title: Email/Password vs Google Sign-In
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs to consider when choosing providers

narration.text: Choosing between Email/Password and Google Sign-In involves UX, reach, and implementation trade-offs. Email/Password works everywhere and gives you explicit control over account creation; it requires validating input, enforcing password strength, and providing recovery flows. Google Sign-In offers faster onboarding for users with Google accounts and can increase conversions because there is less typing, but it requires additional Console OAuth configuration and the google_sign_in package. A common mix is to offer both: allow email signup for users who prefer it while offering Google as a convenience. Concretely, a user who wants privacy or doesn't have a Google account will register with email, while another user will choose Google for one-tap access. Misconception: Google Sign-In always simplifies auth — it reduces friction but increases surface area for platform-specific client ID and consent configuration. Another consideration is session clearing: with Google you must explicitly clear the Google session on sign-out to avoid silent re-sign-ins. Takeaway: use Email/Password for universal support and add Google to improve conversion, but account for platform and configuration steps. Email/Password vs Google Sign-In means email/password is universal and under your control; google improves onboarding but requires extra console setup and provider session handling.. In practical terms, trade-offs to consider when choosing providers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Email/password is universal and under your control; Google improves onboarding but requires extra Console setup and provider session handling.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Comparison
Email / Password
  • Works across platforms; no external provider required.
  • Requires password policies and recovery flows.
  • Easy to enable in Firebase Console with a toggle.
Google Sign-In
  • Simpler onboarding for users with Google accounts.
  • Needs google_sign_in, OAuth client IDs, and consent configuration.
  • Remember to sign out of GoogleSignIn to clear local sessions.
Recommendation
Offer both: provide email/password for universality and Google for convenience, and handle provider setup and sign-out explicitly.

screens.title: Implementation Roadmap
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step plan to add authentication to your app

narration.text: Follow a clear implementation roadmap to add authentication safely. Step one: enable Email/Password and Google in the Firebase Console and confirm OAuth details. Step two: add dependencies — firebase_core, firebase_auth, and google_sign_in — to pubspec. yaml, and run flutter pub get. Step three: initialize Firebase in main with Firebase. initializeApp and only then create your AuthWrapper that subscribes to authStateChanges. Step four: implement AuthScreen with controllers and try-catch wrappers for createUserWithEmailAndPassword and signInWithEmailAndPassword, showing clear error messages for common codes. Step five: implement signInWithGoogle using google_sign_in and signInWithCredential, handling cancellation and errors. Step six: implement signOut that calls FirebaseAuth. instance. signOut and provider signOut when needed. Finally, test the end-to-end flow: register, sign in, view HomeScreen with currentUser information, and sign out to observe the UI transition. screens.subtitle: Map codes to user-facing messages for a robust experience

narration.text: FirebaseAuthException provides error codes and messages you should map to friendly UI text. Key codes you will see include weak-password, email-already-in-use, invalid-email, user-not-found, and wrong-password. For example, when createUserWithEmailAndPassword throws weak-password you should inform the user to pick a stronger password and optionally suggest rules. When signInWithEmailAndPassword throws user-not-found, suggest registering or checking the email address. A common novice mistake is displaying raw exception messages returned by Firebase; they can be technical and confusing. Instead, switch on e. code and show tailored hints or recovery steps, such as offering a password reset when wrong-password is encountered repeatedly. Also log full exception details to your development console for debugging while keeping the UI messages simple. Misconception to avoid: an authentication exception is not always a code bug — sometimes it signals a missing provider in the Console, so inspect configuration when encountering unexpected codes. Takeaway: treat FirebaseAuthException as your control flow for graceful error recovery and clear user guidance. screens.title: Practical Tips and Common Pitfalls
screens.subtitle: Initialize, await, dispose, and test thoroughly

narration.text: A few practical tips make authentication smooth in production. First, initialize Firebase in main before creating widgets that access Firebase services. Second, always await asynchronous calls for registration, sign-in, sign-out, and token exchange so the UI reflects the final state. Third, dispose TextEditingController instances in stateful widgets to avoid memory leaks. Fourth, test both registration and sign-in flows and verify that authStateChanges transitions are correctly handled. Fifth, test cancellation paths for Google Sign-In and handle null authentication objects gracefully. A common pitfall is relying on FirebaseAuth. instance. currentUser immediately after a sign-in call without awaiting — this leads to null reads and UI errors. Another frequent issue is missing Console configuration for Google OAuth; it looks like a code issue but is configuration. For testing, register, sign in, sign out, and attempt error cases like weak passwords or wrong passwords to ensure your error messages are helpful. Takeaway: a disciplined approach to initialization, awaiting, disposal, and configuration avoids most authentication bugs you will encounter.
